title: Concurrency: Correct Shared Counter
contract: Two worker threads each increment a shared counter times times; times ≥ 0. Return the exact total after joining. Compare monitor locking and AtomicInteger; never use a racy counter as a valid baseline.
brute: int[] counter={0};Object lock=new Object();Runnable work=()->{for(int i=0;i<times;i++)synchronized(lock){counter[0]++;}};Thread a=new Thread(work),b=new Thread(work);a.start();b.start();join(a);join(b);emit("Both workers joined; every increment held the monitor","increments per worker",times,"counter",counter[0]);return counter[0];
optimal: java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger counter=new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger();Runnable work=()->{for(int i=0;i<times;i++)counter.incrementAndGet();};Thread a=new Thread(work),b=new Thread(work);a.start();b.start();join(a);join(b);emit("Both workers joined; atomic read-modify-write preserves updates","increments per worker",times,"counter",counter.get());return counter.get();
reasoning: A synchronized monitor makes the read-modify-write operation indivisible and establishes visibility between critical sections.
AtomicInteger supplies an atomic increment for this single-variable invariant, avoiding an explicit monitor in the application code.

Both approaches are correct; neither is universally faster. This animation records deterministic before/after checkpoints, not a fabricated thread schedule. Joining is essential before reading the final count; volatile alone does not make ++ atomic.
complexity: O(t) increments excluding scheduling/contention, O(1) shared data
O(t) increment calls; retry cost depends on contention, O(1) shared data
